new_statements.quote: Primary and secondary stress are indicated by acute and grave accents respectively, although neither is phonemic. [...] Plains Miwok syllables are of the following types, where C represents any consonant and V stands for any vowel: CV, CVC, CV·, and CV·C. Primary stress usually falls on the first long syllable, where CVC, CV·, and CV·C all count as long syllables, but there is much fluctuation. It may shift to a final long syllable in disyllabic or trisyllabic words, in which case there will usually be a secondary stress on the vacated syllable. Primary stress frequently occurs on the penult of trisyllabic stems even if the penult is short, and it may shift to that position in longer stems. Alternations like the following are common: ʔíkoʔ tajòkák ≈ ʔìkoʔ tajókák 'They've gone running.' ʔumúnaj ≈ ʔumùnáj 'girl'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic. Primary stress normally falls on the first heavy syllable of the word, where heavy = closed (CVC), long-vowelled (CV·) or both (CV·C); light = CV. But placement fluctuates: in two- and three-syllable words it may move to a final heavy syllable (leaving secondary stress on the vacated syllable), and in trisyllabic (and longer) stems it frequently sits on the penult even when the penult is light. Callaghan 1972 (General Linguistics 12) states the same in shorter form: first long syllable regularly stressed in Eastern Miwok, 'although stress may shift to the penult in Plains Miwok and Northern Sierra Miwok'; Callaghan 2014: 112 uses 'first closed syllable' as the stress locus.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Marked with grave accent; 'there will usually be a secondary stress on the vacated syllable' when primary stress shifts rightward (e.g. ʔìkoʔ tajókák). No general secondary-stress rule stated for Plains Miwok (a rhythmic rule on succeeding long syllables is given for Sierra Miwok).
new_statements.exceptions: 'much fluctuation'; shift to final heavy syllable in di-/trisyllabic words; penult stress on trisyllabic stems even if the penult is short, and optionally in longer stems; free alternations in the same word (ʔumúnaj ≈ ʔumùnáj). Earlier Callaghan (1960s UCPL/IJAL) called Plains Miwok stress phonemic; the 1972 and 1987 statements supersede that.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('first long syllable' of the word; 'disyllabic or trisyllabic words', 'trisyllabic stems'); examples are sentence forms in transcription with acute/grave marks. Data are Callaghan's 1960s field data from the last speakers; no phrasal or citation-form distinction is drawn. Note also that Callaghan 1984 (Plains Miwok Dictionary intro) has not been opened and is the fuller primary statement to check.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1987 chapter and the 1984 dictionary describe Plains Miwok proper (Callaghan's own field data from the last speakers, Sacramento-San Joaquin delta; = plai1259, ISO pmw). Callaghan 1972 covers Plains Miwok inside a Miwok-wide statement; Callaghan 1971 (Saclan paper) gives the Sierra Miwok rule, not Plains Miwok. No dialect distinctions are drawn in any source seen.
